This page demonstrates the local distribution-regression estimator for regression-discontinuity (RD)
designs. The estimator follows Frandsen, Frölich & Melly (2012) and targets the quantile treatment
effect for local compliers at the cutoff. It handles both sharp and fuzzy designs: the sharp design
is the special case in which the treatment probability jumps from zero to one.

The estimator estimates the complier distribution functions of the treated and untreated potential
outcomes by local-linear weighted least squares on the running variable, separately on either side
of the cutoff. The quantile effects are the differences between the inverses of those two
distribution functions. The implementation mirrors Stata's `rddqte`: the outcome grid is built from
weighted quantiles of the local sample, the estimated CDFs are rearranged by sorting, and the
quantiles are read off the inverted CDFs.

A bandwidth must be supplied. The estimator does not select one internally. `outcome_grid` is either
the number of weighted-quantile points used for the distribution regressions or an explicit sequence
of outcome values.

{{< include _setup-rdd.qmd >}}

```{python}
#| label: setup
import polars as pl

from qte.bootstrap import BootstrapConfig, BootstrapMultiplierConfig
from qte.names import EFFECT_ID, QUANTILE_ID
from qte.rdd import (
    LocalPolynomialConfig,
    RunningVariableConfig,
    estimate_rdd_distribution_effects,
    get_true_first_stage,
    get_true_local_effects,
    simulate_rdd_data,
)

QS = [0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 0.90]
BOOTSTRAP = BootstrapConfig(n_iter=20, seed=42, n_workers=2)
UNIFORM_BOOTSTRAP = BootstrapMultiplierConfig(n_draws=200, seed=42)
```

## Simulated fuzzy design

The simulation follows the Monte Carlo model in the paper. The running variable is normal, the
treatment effect is heterogeneous and equal to `-eps_1`, and exceeding the cutoff lowers the cost of
treatment. Treatment is possible on both sides of the cutoff, so the design is fuzzy.

```{python}
#| label: simulate
ds = simulate_rdd_data(n=50_000, alpha=2.5, seed=42)
ds.head()
```

The true complier effects and the population first stage are available from the simulation helpers.

```{python}
#| label: truth
truth, true_late = get_true_local_effects(QS, alpha=2.5, seed=1)
truth
```

```{python}
#| label: first-stage
get_true_first_stage(alpha=2.5)
```

## Estimation

```{python}
#| label: estimate
res = estimate_rdd_distribution_effects(
    ds,
    outcome="y",
    treatment="treatment",
    running_variable=RunningVariableConfig("running", 0.0),
    qs=QS,
    local_polynomial_config=LocalPolynomialConfig(bandwidth=0.5),
    outcome_grid=100,
    bootstrap_config=BOOTSTRAP,
)

res.qtt
```

The point estimates should be close to the simulated truth. The first stage is the estimated jump in
the treatment probability at the cutoff.

```{python}
#| label: compare
res.qtt.select(QUANTILE_ID, EFFECT_ID).with_columns(pl.Series("truth", truth[EFFECT_ID]))
```

```{python}
#| label: late
res.att
```

## Uniform Bands

Passing a `BootstrapMultiplierConfig` switches to multiplier draws. With `degree=2` this is the
CHS-style local-quadratic fit. The pointwise SEs and the uniform critical value come from the same
draws. `band="sup-t"` uses the studentised sup-t critical value; `band="uniform"` uses the CHS/Stata
constant-width band.

```{python}
#| label: uniform
uniform_res = estimate_rdd_distribution_effects(
    ds,
    outcome="y",
    treatment="treatment",
    running_variable=RunningVariableConfig("running", 0.0),
    qs=QS,
    local_polynomial_config=LocalPolynomialConfig(bandwidth=0.5, degree=2),
    outcome_grid=60,
    bootstrap_config=UNIFORM_BOOTSTRAP,
)

uniform_res.uniform_sup_t_critical_value(0.95)
```

```{python}
#| label: uniform-plot
show_chart(uniform_res.plot(band="sup-t"))
```

## Design Plots

The outcome against the running variable, with binned means and local-linear fits on each side of
the cutoff:

```{python}
#| label: design-plot
show_chart(res.plot_design(ds, n_bins=20))
```

The treatment probability against the running variable shows the first stage:

```{python}
#| label: treatment-plot
show_chart(res.plot_treatment(ds, n_bins=20))
```

## Presentation

```{python}
#| label: plot
show_chart(res.plot())
```
